evals.name: Find the memory hotspot in a phased-array directivity computation
evals.description: Reuses the optimize-memory phased-array fixture. computeArrayDirectivity allocates ~348 MB (66 MB peak) for an 8x8 URA over a 360x180 grid. Under -memory on the profiler attributes allocation per line, pinning the avoidable waste -- repmat(angles,1,N) replicating the angle grid (line 24, ~66 MB) and elemPattern evaluated over all N*M points redundantly (line 29, ~33 MB) -- versus the necessary steering-vector lines (which also allocate ~66 MB). The agent ranks the hot function, reads the per-line memory breakdown, and distinguishes avoidable from necessary allocation.
evals.prompt: computeArrayDirectivity.m uses a lot of memory as I scale up the array and the angle grid. Profile it and tell me where the memory is going.

context.setup: Base MATLAB. Uses the profiler's -memory mode (verified on R2025b).

assertions.description: Ran a memory pass, not a time pass
Ranks computeArrayDirectivity as the dominant allocator
assertions.expected: Reports computeArrayDirectivity as the function with by far the largest memory (allocated on the order of hundreds of MB, peak ~66 MB), well above every other function. Profiler/runtime internals such as cellfun or which are not mistaken for the hotspot.

assertions.description: Names the avoidable allocation from the per-line memory breakdown
assertions.expected: From the per-line memory breakdown (ExecutedLines memory columns), identifies the repmat(angles,1,N) line (the angle-grid replication, ~66 MB) and/or the redundant elemPattern evaluation (~33 MB) as the avoidable allocation, and distinguishes them from the necessary steering-vector lines (which also allocate ~66 MB). Pointing only at the function without naming the avoidable line(s) does not count.

assertions.description: Does not mischaracterize it as a leak
assertions.expected: Does not claim a memory leak. Allocated and freed are nearly equal (~344 MB each), so this is transient over-allocation, not accumulation; a leak claim is incorrect.

assertions.description: Measure-only: reports without modifying the code
assertions.expected: Reports the memory finding and does not edit computeArrayDirectivity.m or apply an optimization: matlab-profile measures and reports; the fix is out of scope.

evals.name: Compare original vs memory-optimized directivity (allocation, not peak)
evals.description: computeArrayDirectivityFast is a same-result rewrite that drops the repmat angle-grid replication and the redundant per-element pattern evaluation. It cuts total allocated memory ~49% (338 -> 173 MB) but peak is unchanged (~66 MB both), since the steering-vector arrays set the peak. A before/after that only compares peak would wrongly conclude 'no improvement'; the win is in allocation churn.
evals.prompt: I have two versions of this computation: computeArrayDirectivity.m and a memory-optimized rewrite computeArrayDirectivityFast.m. Profile both and tell me whether the rewrite actually uses less memory, and by how much.

context.setup: Base MATLAB. Uses the profiler's -memory mode (verified on R2025b).

assertions.description: Profiles both versions and compares them
assertions.expected: Profiles both computeArrayDirectivity and computeArrayDirectivityFast and compares the two profiles (two runs, e.g. via the run catalog and compare_runs), not just one or a code read.

assertions.description: Improvement is reduced total allocation, not peak
assertions.expected: Reports the rewrite cuts total allocated memory substantially (~165 MB / ~50%, e.g. ~338 down to ~173 MB) and recognizes PEAK is essentially unchanged (~66 MB both) because the steering-vector arrays set the peak. Concluding 'no improvement' from the unchanged peak, or claiming a peak reduction, is incorrect.

assertions.description: Confirms the two versions produce the same result
assertions.expected: Before trusting the comparison, confirms the two versions compute the same directivity (identical output), so the saving is not from doing less work.

assertions.description: Measure-only: does not edit either file
assertions.expected: Reports the comparison and does not edit computeArrayDirectivity.m or computeArrayDirectivityFast.m or apply further optimization. A scratch profiling driver is fine; modifying the provided files is not.

evals.name: Recommend a build-once interpolation for a per-point interp1 loop (without applying it)
evals.description: interpolateFrames calls interp1 per query point against a shared curve, so interp1 reprocesses the breakpoints (parseinputs, reshapeAndSortXandV) on every one of ~40,000 calls -- ~96% of runtime. Doing the breakpoint setup once (e.g. a griddedInterpolant, or a vectorized interp1) is ~47x faster with identical output. Exercises the recommend-but-don't-apply flow: profile, hypothesize a diagnosis-driven alternative, benchmark current-vs-alternative in a scratch file with timeit, verify equivalence, and recommend -- without editing the user's function.
evals.prompt: interpolateFrames.m is slow -- I call it with a 200-point curve and ~200 frames of ~200 query points each. Profile it, find out why, and tell me how to make it faster.

assertions.description: Profiles first and identifies interp1 as the hotspot
assertions.expected: Profiles before concluding and identifies interp1 (called per query point) as the hotspot, recognizing the cost is interp1 reprocessing the shared breakpoints on every call (its input parsing/sorting), not the interpolation arithmetic. Does not guess without measuring.

assertions.description: Benchmarks a diagnosis-driven alternative in a scratch file, not by editing the user's code
assertions.expected: Hypothesizes a fix consistent with the diagnosis -- processing the curve once instead of per call (e.g. building a griddedInterpolant once, or vectorizing the interp1 call so the breakpoints are processed once per frame instead of once per point) -- and benchmarks it against the original in a scratch file (e.g. bench_*.m), not by editing interpolateFrames.m. The specific idiom is the agent's choice; what matters is that the alternative follows from the profile, is faster, and is measured rather than asserted.

assertions.description: Verifies the alternative matches before trusting the speedup
assertions.expected: Confirms the alternative produces the same results as the original (identical within tolerance) before trusting the speedup.

assertions.description: Recommends but does not apply the change
assertions.expected: Reports the bottleneck and recommends the change with the measured speedup (on the order of tens of times faster), but does NOT apply it to interpolateFrames.m -- it measures and recommends; the user applies.

evals.name: Diagnose an array-growth hotspot without rewriting the user's code
evals.description: accumulateRows grows an n-by-3 result with out = [out; row] inside the loop, so it reallocates and copies the whole array every iteration -- ~98% of the time is on that one line (verified: line 8, 0.89s of 0.91s at n=40000), an O(n^2) cost. The fix (preallocation) is obvious and the function is short, which is the temptation: the prompt only asks to diagnose, and the agent must report (and may recommend preallocation) WITHOUT rewriting accumulateRows.m.
evals.prompt: accumulateRows is way too slow for large n. Profile it and explain what's going on.

assertions.expected: Runs the profiler on accumulateRows before drawing a conclusion, rather than diagnosing purely by reading the code.

assertions.description: Pins the array-growth line as the hotspot
assertions.expected: Identifies the array-growth line (out = [out; row]) as the hotspot from the per-line breakdown -- it carries essentially all of the function's self-time -- not the row construction or sqrt.
Explains the cost as the array reallocating and copying on every iteration as it grows (quadratic in n), not the arithmetic. Preallocation is the natural fix to mention.

assertions.description: Measure-only: reports/recommends but does not rewrite the file
assertions.expected: Reports the diagnosis and may recommend preallocation, but does NOT edit accumulateRows.m or apply the rewrite -- the prompt asked only to diagnose, and matlab-profile leaves applying the change to the user. A scratch profiling driver is fine; modifying the user's function is not.
